scenes.name: Arrive and settle on a sideways track
scenes.look: A held row slides sideways with the scroll and each item's height and tilt come from where it is on screen, so the letters of one giant closing line enter scattered at the right edge, swoop through their line and settle by the middle (the letters already on screen when the section arrives swoop within under half the letter size, so the line reads at once); then the camera pulls back until the whole line fits, ending on a calm frame with the line whole and a button. Its default is the page's last word and its action; the stair preset makes it a staircase of testimonials and the rise preset a short track of projects.

The end frame shows the whole line, verb included: read the 100% frame at 1440, 768 and 390, and if it rests on the last words alone, shorten the line or set it smaller. scenes.name: Closing cut under the rise
scenes.look: In the last section the one thing the page is about stands, as a cut-out masked from the closing photograph itself, in a flat room of two tints: that photograph's own wall and floor, split exactly on the row where its floor meets its wall, the cut-out starting low on the flat floor. From the first frame a carrier lifts it steadily up the frame, whole on every frame and never sliced by the top edge, onto the row where the thing stands in the picture, while the stage counter-moves a fifth of a screen down and back at most, so the camera seems to duck under the rise. There, in one frame and under the motion, the flat room and the cut-out are gone and the full-bleed closing photograph that was waiting beneath fills the screen, the same thing in the same place and the floor line on the same row, so the cut reads as the room coming into focus rather than a jump; the camera's return carries on through it. On a short flat band of the floor's tint at its foot the page's last sentence arrives in two or three whole phrases, the one plain action together with the last, and the frame rests finished for about the last tenth of the hold.
scenes.reduced: The finished composition: the markup as the page writes it, nothing moving.
scenes.phone: The same rise and cut at full width: the cut-out fitted to the width less 16px margins, starting low and rising whole onto the subject's place in the portrait crop, the closing photograph's own portrait crop with its own floor line and the subject whole, a shallower dip (phoneDip 0.1, lowered where it would sink the subject's foot under the band) so the crop keeps its height and the subject stays whole above the band, the line over the action on the short band at the foot, the caption left out (it would sit on the cut-out). phone: 'rest' gives the finished composition, the closing photograph a screen tall with the band, the line and the action.
scenes.place: The end of the page: the order, the booking or the visit, straight after one quiet section. The footer after it is a designed section of its own and follows the finished frame: leave `foot` unset (it pulls the element it names over the stage's foot, so it suits only a page that ends on the scene). Once per page, never right after another scene. Pages that sell or show one ordinary physical thing: a teapot, a jug, a stool, a lamp, a bottle, a dish, a garment.
scenes.content: One full-colour closing photograph of the subject in place: the very object standing clear of its surroundings (a distinct colour or a plain ground behind it, so it can be masked) on a floor, a table top or a counter that meets the wall, trees or sky behind on a clear line, with a calm area or room at its foot for a short band; landscape 2400px wide or more, and a portrait crop as its own <source> in which the subject stays whole (or one file framed with --ccr-object-portrait). The rising cut-out is masked from that same photograph (keyed or traced, transparent PNG or WebP, the object only, nothing of the table under it), so the cut lands the very thing back in its own room; never a drawing, never a second photograph of a lookalike. On the img and each <source>: data-horizon (that file's floor line, 0-1) and data-subject (the subject's centre across and its foot, 0-1). scenes.name: A still closing line in a field of words
scenes.look: The closing section holds one line still at the lower left of a calm ground, at display size in two lines with the page's one action after its last word, while a stream of single short words (the places, dishes, materials or services the page is about) comes out of a vanishing point above it: each word appears at a readable size, grows quickly in one flat ink as it travels out along one of six to eight fixed lanes, and fades to nothing while it is still whole on screen, so no word is ever cut by the edge and at most six are drawn at once. The last word grows out of the same point while a last wave is still passing; it stops at its full size over the closing line and stays as the section's heading. Each lane is a wedge round the vanishing point and every word grows about that point, so no word ever touches another, the line, the action or the heading, and nothing is searched. Opacity and scale only: no blur, no 3D layers; the field is hidden from screen readers. For a page with no pictures, or none to spare for its close.

scenes.name: Closing object turns over
scenes.look: In the last screen the one object the page is about, a cut-out photograph of something flat (a book, a card, a ticket, a box lid, a label), rises from below, square, with a slight drift to one side and settles flat and whole; then, over the middle of the scroll, it tips back, comes a little nearer and up, and turns over about its horizontal axis from -180 to 0 degrees in CSS 3D, edge-on half-way, while the closing ground comes up behind it as one flat, hard-edged field whose edge crosses the object's axis at edge-on. It settles as the scroll runs out, showing its plain other face set in the page's own type: the closing line at display size across the face, the one action right under it, and a sentence and a colophon on its bottom edge. The scene ends on the object showing its other side.

The footer after it is a designed section of its own and follows the finished frame: leave `foot` unset (it pulls the element it names over the stage's foot, so it suits only a page that ends on the scene). Once per page, never right after another scene. Calm pages that sell or show one physical thing: a book, an edition, a ticket, a print, a product in its box.
scenes.content: One photograph of the object's front, straight on and cut to its own edges (no background, no shadow, no table left in the crop), 1200px tall or more, its width and height set on the img; best between 0.72 and 0.9 wide to 1 tall (a book, a card, a box lid), which fills a phone at full width and a desktop at about 92% of its height. The front must differ clearly from the plain face (colour, pattern, a picture on it), or the turn does not read. The other face: a closing line of 3-5 words on two lines, its longest line about 10 letters so it can run across the face at display size; the one action of 2-4 words right under it (a booking, an order, a download; never an email address or a phone number); then, on the face's lower edge, an optional sentence of 10-20 words and a colophon of 4-10 words naming what the front shows. scenes.name: Panels re-proportion as they arrive
scenes.look: A short statement holds at display size in a solid column of the page's ground on the left, as tall as the stage, while four to six large panels arrive one at a time beside it, about 0.4 screens of scroll each. Every panel is one picture over a band of the page's own ground. A panel arrives in the main slot (about 42% of the width) split half and half with its name on one line; as the reader scrolls, the picture grows by its clip to 70% and pushes the band down, and the name re-sets onto two lines in large type, so each item visibly comes into focus at full size. When the next panel comes, a hand-over runs on a clock: the settled panel steps left into a narrower slot beside the column, still whole and named, the one before it slides away whole behind the column, and the next slides in from the right. So the screen holds at most two panels, never a strip of one, and every frame after the first settle shows one panel settled whole. The first panel, with nothing settled beside it, arrives across the whole window and narrows into the slot when the second comes. The last frame is the last panel settled; the column's foot holds the sentence and the one action as a plain button on the page ground. All panels share one ground and one ink; only the pictures tell them apart. For a school's programmes, a developer's buildings, a publisher's imprints, a studio's services: four or five parallel places or offers with one strong picture each.

scenes.name: Window names its parts
scenes.look: The product's own window takes stock of itself. On a held stage the window, built in HTML from 12 to 18 separate flat parts on the page ground (a frame, a sidebar, a header, figure blocks, rows, buttons), sits beside a short list that has only its heading. Under the scroll the window steps back to about 0.92 and tips about 15 degrees in CSS 3D while its parts lift apart in depth tier by tier (sidebar and header a little, figure blocks more, rows further, buttons furthest), shown only by the gaps between them, never by shadows. Then a solid band in the accent crosses the window from left to right, behind every part's words; each part it reaches turns to the accent for a beat (a fill, never an outline) while its plain sentence-case name, said as what it does for the user, drops into the next slot of the list, one row at a time. Last, the parts settle flat and the tilt eases out, the list complete beside the window. The visitor watches the product name its parts instead of reading feature copy. Unlike parts lock into the whole, nothing flies in: the screen is whole from the first frame and the scene names it; unlike the product replay, no task is played, no query typed and no cursor drawn.

scenes.name: Window relay with a trail of stamps

The window leaves a stamp-sized box open in the opposite corner, where the old picture stays on top and shrinks into its stamp, then slides out whole into a trail of stamps along the bottom edge of the caption band, which moves one place along (four at most, the oldest leaving at the far end).
